turn_text: What makes a woman truly iconic? Breaking barriers and shattering glass ceilings, overcoming incredible obstacles, defying standards and expectations. Some women are dangerous and even downright deadly. This is the Iconic Women Podcast, and I'm your host, Sarah. Each episode I'm here to share another woman's incredible story. Let's dive in. Today's iconic woman is a modern day warrior woman. Tammy Duckworth of the USA. She's known for a lot of firsts, but the thing she's most well known for is being the first female double amputee from the Iraq War in 2004. Tammy was born in Thailand to an American father and Thai mother and she's considered a natural born citizen of the USA. Her father was a veteran of the US Army and US Marine Corps and their family history goes all the way back to serving in the American Revolution. Education was always a priority for Tammy. She skipped the ninth grade and received a bachelor's in political science, a master of arts in international affairs, and was working toward her PhD when her program was interrupted by her war service. She did later go on to complete her PhD in human services in 2015. Tammy joined the US Army Reserve in 1992 and chose to fly helicopters because it was one of the only combat jobs that women were allowed to do at the time. She served in the Iraq war and was co-piloting a helicopter when she was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade in 2004. As a result, she lost her right leg near her hip and her left leg below the knee, officially making her the first American female double amputee from the Iraq war. In addition, the explosion severely broke her right arm and tore tissue from it, resulting in major surgery. Tammy received a Purple Heart, a U.S. military decoration awarded in the name of the president to those wounded or killed while serving in the U.S. military. Despite the severity of her injuries, she sought and obtained a medical waiver that allowed her to continue serving in the Army National Guard until she retired in 2014. Tammy also worked for both Illinois and U.S. Veterans Affairs. She's credited with starting a program in Illinois to help veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD, and veterans with brain injuries. In 2009, she was appointed by President Barack Obama to be the Assistant Secretary of Public and Intergovernmental Affairs for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. She coordinated a joint initiative with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to help end veteran homelessness, worked to address the unique challenges faced by female as well as Native American veterans, and created the Office of Online Communications to improve the VA's accessibility, especially among young veterans. In 2012, Tammy was elected to Congress in the U.S. House of Representatives, and so she became the first person born in Thailand elected to Congress, the first Thai American woman elected to Congress, the first woman with a disability elected to Congress, and the first Asian American from Illinois in Congress. In 2016, Tammy went on to run for a Senate seat, and she won. Only one other female Asian American senator had been elected before her, and she was the first female double amputee in the Senate as well. During her time in the 115th Congress as part of the Senate, Tammy is credited with saving the Americans with Disabilities Act, a civil rights law that prohibits discrimination based on disability. She's recognized by the Veterans Service Organization and the Paralyzed Veterans of America for her leadership in defending the ADA. In 2018, Tammy gave birth to her youngest daughter and became the first senator to give birth while holding office. Shortly afterward, the Senate passed a resolution, introduced and led by Tammy, to change Senate rules to allow senators to bring a child under one year old onto the Senate floor in order to breastfeed. The day after that resolution passed, Tammy's daughter became the first baby on the Senate floor, and Tammy became the first Senator to cast a vote while holding a baby. There are so many things that make Tammy Duckworth iconic. She's overcome incredible obstacles and also broken innumerable barriers. She's an unstoppable force in her courage and determination to fight forward. Representation matters, and the significance of a woman with a visible physical disability in US Congress is critical. Not just because we need her voice and so many other voices too at the table, when things like the Americans with Disabilities Act are being threatened, but also because she represents to so many kids and adults across the country that their voices matter and there's a place for them at the table where decisions are being made. Furthermore, she defies so many stereotypes as a survivor from a war injury, as a combat helicopter veteran. Basically, she's one tough cookie, and we can all use a little inspiration and motivation from stories like hers. So what can we learn from her example? Don't be afraid of being the first person to do something. Just because it's never been done before doesn't mean you can't be the first to do it. More and more women are being represented in Congress, and it took Tammy's leadership and influence to amplify their voices as mothers to prioritize things like being able to breastfeed at work. Just the pressure that women already feel in every industry to make choices between motherhood and work. Preachers that men do not experience in any way to the same extent are slightly alleviated by the example that Tammy set by being the first Senator to give birth while in office. Role models like Tammy help us believe that we can have it all and that our voices matter and our needs matter. Your whole life, people will tell you you can't do things. that it's never been done before, or that it just isn't done that way. But hopefully, Tammy's story can help us push back against those criticisms and push forward to fight for what we believe in, and to be brave enough to be the first. Now she's iconic. Can't get enough? Find us on Facebook, facebook.com slash iconic women podcast. If you love this podcast, make sure you subscribe and don't forget to leave a review. Thanks so much for listening and I'll catch you next time.
